title: Queen against pawn: the draws
summary: The two pawns that escape the staircase of checks: stalemate in the corner, the zone where the king still wins, and the traps on both sides.
part.rook.title: Rook pawn: the corner stalemates
part.rook.summary: Why the staircase of checks fails when the pawn is on the a-file.
part.rookZone.title: Rook pawn: a close king wins
part.rookZone.summary: With the king in the zone, the queen lets the pawn promote and mates.
part.bishop.title: Bishop pawn: the other stalemate
part.bishop.summary: The king goes to the corner next to the pawn, and taking the pawn is stalemate.
part.bishopZone.title: Bishop pawn: Lolli and the zone
part.bishopZone.summary: The 1763 study and the rule of the b3 and d2 squares.
part.sides.title: Short side, long side and traps
part.sides.summary: Where the defending king belongs, and the only moves that save the draw.
part.summary.title: Summary
part.summary.summary: Two master games, three rules and a defence in the practical challenge.
step.t_rook: A rook pawn on a2, the black king next to it, our king far away. In the last lesson the staircase of checks drove the black king in front of its pawn and our king won a step. Think: does the staircase work here? What changes with the pawn on the a-file?
step.t_rook.hint1: Try the staircase and see where the black king goes after the last check.
step.t_rook.hint2: Once the black king is on a1, count its moves if the queen stays on b3.
step.rookWhy: This is where the attempt ends. The black king is on a1, in front of its pawn, just as we wanted. But now Black has no move at all: the king can't leave and the pawn can't advance. If the queen stays put, it's stalemate. With a centre pawn the king had the other side of the pawn to step out to. On the a-file there is no other side. So the queen has to release the pressure, the black king returns to b2, and everything starts again.
step.d_rook: Watch the whole staircase and where it gets stuck. White's moves are the ones from the last lesson.
step.d_rook.m1: 1.Qd4+. A check from a distance, heading for the pawn.
step.d_rook.m2: The king goes to b1. It was the only move that didn't lose: on the other squares the queen would win the pawn.
step.d_rook.m4: 2...Kc2. The king steps out but keeps an eye on the pawn.
step.d_rook.m7: 4.Qb3+. Now the black king seems forced in front of the pawn.
step.d_rook.m8: 4...Ka1! It goes, and it's stalemate unless the queen moves away. White has gained nothing: a draw.
step.rookHold: Now you defend with Black. The queen has just given check on d4. Put your king on the right square each move until it reaches the corner.
step.rookHold.hint: The king must not move away from the pawn. And when there is no other square, the corner on a1 is a hiding place.
step.rookHold.done: 1...Kb1, 2...Kc2, 3...Kb1 and 4...Ka1. In the end your king is stuck in the corner and White can't get it out without stalemate. That's a draw.
step.t_rookZone: The same pawn on a2, but now our king is on d5. Think: is it close enough? How do you win if the staircase doesn't work?
step.t_rookZone.hint1: You don't have to stop the pawn from promoting. Ask what happens afterwards.
step.t_rookZone.hint2: With the white king on b3, the queen has two mating squares near the corner.
step.rookZoneWhy: The marked squares are the zone: with the white king on any of them, and the queen giving check, White wins. From there the king reaches b3 in at most two moves, or d3 and d2 in one. The idea is new: instead of holding the pawn back, we let it promote. The new queen is stuck in the corner, and our king and queen mate before it can do anything.
step.d_rookZone: The white king on d5 is in the zone. Watch the queen gain a tempo and the king head for b3.
step.d_rookZone.m1: 1.Qf6+. A check along the long diagonal, which already watches a1.
step.d_rookZone.m3: 2.Qf1+. The queen comes to the first rank.
step.d_rookZone.m5: 3.Qe2+. The queen stays close, on the second rank.
step.d_rookZone.m7: 4.Kc4! It looks like a mistake: the pawn may promote.
step.d_rookZone.m9: 5.Kb3! Now White threatens mate on c2 or on d1, and the new queen, locked in the corner behind its own king, can't cover those squares.
step.rookKb3: Look at this position calmly. Does Black have a queen against a queen? Not really: Black has a queen locked on a1. The white king on b3 takes a2, b2 and c2 from the black king, and the white queen threatens 2.Qc2 or 2.Qd1, both mate. The black queen can't cover everything in time; at most it gives itself up with a check. This is the picture to remember.
step.rookZoneMove: Your turn. The white king is on e4, in the zone, and the black king on b1. With checks, bring the black king back to b1, then let the pawn promote at the right moment.
step.rookZoneMove.hint: Checks that keep the black king near the corner. When it is back on b1 with your queen on d2, your king goes to a square that protects c2.
step.rookZoneMove.done: 1.Qb3+, 2.Qd1+, 3.Qd2+ and 4.Kd3. If the pawn promotes, 5.Qc2 is mate. If it becomes a knight to cover c2, the king goes to c3 and the mate comes anyway.
step.t_bishop: Now a bishop pawn on c2, with the black king on b2. Our king is on e4, near the centre. Think: does the staircase work? If not, where is Black's trick?
step.t_bishop.hint1: The a1 corner isn't in front of the pawn, but it's right next to it.
step.t_bishop.hint2: Picture the black king on a1 and the white queen on b3. What happens if the queen takes the pawn?
step.bishopWhy: This is the bishop pawn's trick. The black king hides on a1. If the queen takes on c2, the king has no square at all: a2, b1 and b2 are all covered. Stalemate. And if the queen doesn't take, the pawn promotes. So the queen has to let the king out again, and White never gains the time to bring the king over.
step.d_bishop: The staircase against the bishop pawn. Watch where the black king runs.
step.d_bishop.m2: 1...Ka1! The king goes to the corner instead of leaving the pawn.
step.d_bishop.m7: 4.Qc3+. The queen tries the other diagonal.
step.d_bishop.m9: 5.Qb3+. The same check that worked against the centre pawn.
step.d_bishop.m10: 5...Ka1! And 6.Qxc2 is stalemate. The white king never left e4: a draw.
step.bishopHold: You defend with Black. The queen has given check on b6. Keep your king next to the pawn and use the corner when you need it.
step.bishopHold.hint: Running towards the a1 corner is safe. Running the other way, away from the corner, lets the queen pin the pawn.
step.bishopHold.done: Your king stayed between a1 and b1 the whole time, on the corner side. With the queen on b3 and the king on a1, taking the pawn is stalemate. A draw.
step.t_lolli: A position from 1763. The black king is on d1, on the long side of the pawn, far from the a1 corner. Our king is on g4. Think: how do you keep the black king out of the corner, and how do you bring your king over?
step.t_lolli.hint1: First shut the door: the black king wants to reach b1 or b2.
step.t_lolli.hint2: Then the white king walks. If the pawn promotes while the white king is close, there is a mate with the queen on e2.
step.bishopZoneWhy: Against a bishop pawn the zone is smaller. With the black king on b2, White wins if the king can reach b3 or d2 in a single move: these are the marked squares, a4, b4, c4, d3, e3, d2, e2 and e1. From e4 here it is one step outside the zone. One step too far and stalemate saves Black. That's why the side the black king stands on matters so much.
step.d_lolli: Giambattista Lolli's study from 1763. The black king is on the long side, and the queen won't let it cross.
step.d_lolli.m1: 1.Qb3! The queen watches b1 and c2 and cuts the road to the corner.
step.d_lolli.m2: 1...Kd2. The black king stays on the long side.
step.d_lolli.m3: 2.Qb2. The queen holds the pawn and keeps watching the corner.
step.d_lolli.m5: 3.Kf3! The king comes. If the pawn promotes now, 4.Qe2 is mate.
step.d_lolli.m7: 4.Kf2. Closer, and the king now covers e1.
step.d_lolli.m9: 5.Qd4+. The check pushes the king in front of the pawn.
step.d_lolli.m11: 6.Qb4! A quiet move. Black is in zugzwang: every move makes things worse.
step.d_lolli.m13: 7.Qe1, mate. The white king on f2 protects the queen.
step.bishopZoneMove: Now you finish it. The black king is on c1, in front of the pawn, and our king arrives along the b-file.
step.bishopZoneMove.hint: The king heads for b3, where it helps with the mate. On the way, the queen pins the pawn.
step.bishopZoneMove.done: 1.Kb4, 2.Qd2 and 3.Kb3. If the pawn promotes, 4.Qa2 is mate; if it becomes a knight with check, the king steps out of check and the mate comes anyway. That's the zone at work: the king reached b3.
step.t_trap: You are Black. White has just played Qe2, and the white king is on d5, close but outside the zone. Your king has seven squares. Think: which one draws, and what goes wrong with the others?
step.t_trap.hint1: Remember where the white king wants to go: b3.
step.t_trap.hint2: If the pawn promotes with the white king two steps from b3, White may have time. Look for the square where promoting isn't even needed.
step.trapWhy: Only 1...Ka1 draws. With the king in the corner, White has nothing: 2.Qxc2 is stalemate. On b1 the king looks just as safe, but then 2.Kc4! lets the pawn promote and the white king reaches b3 with mating threats. On c3 the king leaves the corner, and 2.Qe5+ drives it to the long side, where the white king arrives in time. Jesús de la Villa shows this trap in his book: it's the defender's typical mistake.
step.d_trap: Here is the punishment if Black plays Kb1. It's the same Kb3 idea you saw with the rook pawn.
step.d_trap.m1: 1.Kc4! The king heads for b3 and lets the pawn promote.
step.d_trap.m3: 2.Kb3! The king steps out of check and traps the black king on the first rank. Even with a new queen, Black can't escape: it is mate.
step.longSide: The other side of the coin. Here the pawn is on f2 and the black king on e2, on the long side, towards the centre. The short side is the g-file, next to the h1 corner. If the black king reaches g1 or g2, it's the stalemate draw. Only one White move prevents it: 1.Qa6+. The best defence is to go to e1, in front of the pawn, and from there the queen keeps cutting off the g-file while the white king, already on b2, comes closer. The attacker keeps the king on the far side; the defender runs to the short side.
step.trapMove: One more trap, now with the black king on d2, on the long side. White has played Qa2. The white king is on e5. Find the move that holds, and then the next one.
step.trapMove.hint: On d1, the white king would have time to come to d3. Look for a square that keeps the white king away and still protects the pawn.
step.trapMove.done: 1...Kc3! And after 2.Qa1+, 2...Kd2. The black king stays with the pawn without letting the white king in. 1...Kd1 lost to 2.Kd4!, and 1...Kd3 to 2.Qb2, pinning the pawn.
step.t_summary: In the practical challenge, you defend with Black. Think: where does your king go when the queen gives check?
step.t_summary.hint1: Next to the pawn, on the side of the a1 corner.
step.games: This happens among the very best. In 1958 Petrosian and Fischer, two future world champions, agreed a draw in a position where one of them could promote and the other would be left with a bishop pawn on the seventh: both knew it was stalemate. In 1996 Van Wely reached this position against Leko, a whole queen up, and could do nothing: the white king was far away on h7. A draw.
step.recap: Take this with you. One: a rook pawn or a bishop pawn on the seventh, with the defending king next to it, draws by stalemate unless the attacking king is close. Two: close means in the zone. Against a rook pawn, at most two steps from b3, or one step from d3 or d2; against a bishop pawn, one step from b3 or from d2. In the zone, let the pawn promote and mate. Three: the defender takes the king to the short side, the corner side; the attacker doesn't let it cross.
step.finish: Now for real. You have the bishop pawn, the machine has the queen and a distant king. Keep your king next to the pawn, on the corner side, and don't fall for the traps.
ex.e12: White to move. Bishop pawn on f2, the black king on g3, our king far away on h8. Checks get nowhere here. Win.
ex.e12.hint: Look at the square in front of the pawn. Is the black king guarding it?
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qf1! The queen stops in front of the pawn, on a square the black king cannot reach. Now the pawn cannot move, and our king walks over from h8 to take it. Checks such as 1.Qg6+ let the black king reach the corner, and then it was the usual draw. This is the first chapter of TonyRo's study on Lichess: if the queen can stand in front of the pawn, it is over.
ex.e04: Black to move. The white queen is on e1, on the promotion rank. The white king is far away. Which is the only move that draws?
ex.e04.hint: If the king leaves the pawn, the queen will stand in front of it.
ex.e04.solution: 1...c1=Q! The new queen is protected by the king, and after 2.Qxc1+ Kxc1 only the kings are left. Any king move allowed 2.Qc1, the queen blockading the pawn, and the white king would come and take it.
ex.e13: Black to move. The black king is in the a1 corner, but the white king has already reached b3: stalemate no longer saves Black. Only one move draws.
ex.e13.hint: Promoting to a queen loses, and the king has nowhere to go. Look for a new piece that gives check.
ex.e13.solution: 1...c1=N+! The knight checks the king on b3 and attacks the queen on d3 at the same time. The white king has to move, and 2...Nxd3 leaves king and knight against king: a draw. 1...c1=Q? lost to 2.Qa6+ and mate, and 1...Kb1 to 2.Qxc2+. When the king and the queen stand on squares a new knight reaches together, look at the underpromotion.
ex.e10: White to move. Bishop pawn on f2, the black king on e2, not yet in the corner. Our king is on e5. This is a position by Snape. Win.
ex.e10.hint: Checks that keep the black king away from the h1 corner, so our king gains time.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Qc4+ (or 1.Qg4+, 1.Qa2+ or the quiet 1.Qg2) Ke1, 2.Qe4+ Kf1 and 3.Kf4. The black king reaches the corner, but too late: after 3...Kg1 4.Qd4 Kh1, 5.Kg3! and, if the pawn promotes, 6.Qh8+ leads to mate. Qxf2 at any moment with the king on h1 would be stalemate.
ex.e14: White to move. It looks like the bishop pawn draw: the black king on g1, our king on b5, much too far. But Black has an extra pawn on h7. Win.
ex.e14.hint: The h7 pawn can still move. What does that change when the black king goes to the h1 corner?
ex.e14.solution: 1.Qg4+ (or 1.Qg8+) Kh2, 2.Qf3 Kg1, 3.Qg3+ (or 3.Qg4+, 3.Qe3) and, if 3...Kh1, 4.Qxf2. It is not stalemate: Black still has the h7 pawn to move, and against a rook pawn that far back the white king arrives in time. The extra pawn takes the stalemate defence away from Black. Checks along the c-file, such as 1.Qc1+, let the black king go to e2 and d2 and did not win. The position is from Müller and Lamprecht, via Wikipedia.
ex.e16: White to move. Rook pawn on a2, the black king on c3, our king far away on g5. The black king has not reached the corner yet. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e16.hint: Do not check. First take b2 away from the black king, then the long diagonal to the corner.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Qe2! takes b2 away from the black king. After 1...Kb3, 2.Qe5! watches the diagonal down to a1, and after 2...Kc2, 3.Qa1! The queen stands in front of the pawn, and the white king comes to collect it. Checks let the black king reach b2 and a1, and stalemate saved Black. Three quiet moves, and each one is the only win.
ex.e15: White to move. Bishop pawn on c2, the black king on e3, on the long side. Our king is far away on h6. Find the way, one move at a time.
ex.e15.hint: The black king wants to cross to the a1 corner side. Cut him off without checking, then put the queen in front of the pawn.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Qg2! cuts off the second rank: the black king cannot reach d2. After 1...Kd3, 2.Qg5! watches c1 and d2 from a distance, and after 2...Kc3, 3.Qc1! The queen is in front of the pawn and the white king comes to collect it. Checks pushed the black king to b2 and a1, the short side, and that was a draw. It is the idea of the quiet move Qg5 that Wikipedia credits to Flear, here with two more moves.
key.rookDraw: Rook pawn about to queen and the white king far away: when the queen corners the black king, it runs out of moves and it is stalemate. A draw.
key.rookZone: The same pawn, but now the white king is close. It arrives in time, even letting the pawn queen, and mates together with the queen.
key.bishopDraw: Bishop pawn with the white king one step too far away: the black king hides in the corner, and capturing the pawn would leave it stalemated. A draw.
key.lolli: Lolli's study from 1763: the black king is on the side away from the corner. The queen holds the pawn, the white king comes closer and White mates.
key.trap: A trap for Black: only one escape saves the game, going straight to the corner. Any other square lets the queen and the white king close the net.
key.longSide: The black king is on the side away from the corner: there is no stalemate here, and a single well-chosen queen check wins.
key.vanWely: Van Wely against Leko, 1996: the bishop pawn reached the last square but one with the black king in the corner, and the white king was far away. The queen could not win.
key.fischer: The position Petrosian and Fischer saw in 1958: a bishop pawn about to queen and the white king far away. Knowing the queen cannot win, they agreed a draw.
history: Queen against pawn almost always wins. But there are two exceptions every player should know, because they save games that looked lost: the edge pawn and the bishop pawn, when they reach the last square but one with their king beside them and the enemy king is far away. In both cases the defending king hides in the corner, and the queen, unless careful, can only stalemate it. Giambattista Lolli, an eighteenth-century Italian, published a study in 1763 showing when the stronger side's king still arrives in time. In 1958 Petrosian and Fischer agreed a draw because of this stalemate, and in 1996 Van Wely, with the queen, could not beat Leko's bishop pawn. Nearly everything comes down to one count: where the king of the side with the queen is.
practice: Now the exception, with or without a clock. A bishop pawn on the seventh, but your king is close. Keep the black king on the long side and bring your king into the zone.
